papers.caseStudy: Three school bells ring at intervals of 12 minutes, 18 minutes and 30 minutes. They ring together at 9:00 a.m.

solutions.18: By 4: yes, because 64 is divisible by 4. By 8: yes, because 864 is divisible by 8. By 9: yes, because the digit sum is 27. By 11: yes, because (7 + 8 + 4) − (2 + 6) = 11, a multiple of 11.

solutions.22: Other number = (36 × 1,260) ÷ 180 = 252. Since 180 = 2² × 3² × 5 and 252 = 2² × 3² × 7, their HCF is 2² × 3² = 36.

solutions.24: (a) 12 = 2² × 3. (b) LCM(12,18) = 36. (c) LCM(12,18,30) = 2² × 3² × 5 = 180 minutes = 3 hours, so the bells next ring together at 12:00 noon.

notes.subtitle: Eight-Digit Numbers, Estimation & Everyday Measures

concepts.title: Two numeration systems
concepts.text: The Indian system groups digits as ones, thousands, lakhs and crores; the International system groups them as ones, thousands and millions.

concepts.title: Place value and comparison
concepts.text: A digit’s place determines its value. Compare digit counts first, then compare equal-length numbers from the greatest place.

concepts.title: Operations and estimation
concepts.text: Align place values for addition and subtraction. Estimate first so that an unreasonable exact answer is easy to notice.

concepts.title: Length and mass
concepts.text: Convert larger units to smaller units by multiplication before combining measurements.

method: Write the number in a place-value chart.
Insert commas according to the required numeration system.
Estimate the expected size before calculating exactly.
Convert every measurement to one unit and attach the correct unit to the answer.

example.question: Write 6,08,04,025 in the International system and round it to the nearest lakh.
steps: The ten-thousands digit is 0, so 6,08,04,025 rounds down.

practice.question: Find the place value of 7 in 4,72,18,650.
A store receives 325 cartons with 248 items each. Find the total.

tips: Do not read Indian comma groups as International groups.
Keep zeros that hold a place even when their value is zero.
An estimate should be close enough to check the exact answer, not replace it.

notes.subtitle: Number Line, Properties & Identities

concepts.title: Natural and whole numbers
concepts.text: Natural numbers begin at 1 in this course. Whole numbers extend them by including 0.

concepts.title: Number line
concepts.text: Whole numbers increase to the right. Addition moves right and subtraction moves left when the result remains a whole number.

concepts.title: Operation properties
concepts.text: Addition and multiplication are closed, commutative and associative for whole numbers; multiplication distributes over addition and subtraction.

concepts.title: Zero and one
concepts.text: Zero is the additive identity and one is the multiplicative identity. Division by zero is undefined.

formulas: a + b = b + a; a × b = b × a
a × (b + c) = a × b + a × c
method: Identify the operation and the whole numbers involved.
Choose the property that makes the calculation shorter.
Regroup or distribute without changing the value.
Check that the result belongs to the required number set.

example.question: Evaluate 248 × 97 + 248 × 3 efficiently.
steps: Both products contain the common factor 248.

practice.question: Write the first six whole numbers.
Explain why 25 ÷ 0 is undefined.
practice.answer: No number multiplied by 0 can give 25

tips: Subtraction and division are not commutative.
Zero is not the multiplicative identity; multiplying by zero gives zero.
Never assign a value to division by zero.

notes.subtitle: Divisibility, Prime Factors, HCF & LCM

concepts.title: Brackets
concepts.text: Simplify the innermost grouping first, then work outward while preserving every operation sign.

concepts.title: Factors and divisibility
concepts.text: A factor divides exactly; a multiple is obtained by multiplication. Divisibility rules provide quick tests without full division.

concepts.title: Prime factorisation
concepts.text: A prime has exactly two factors. Every composite number has a unique prime-factor product apart from order.

concepts.title: HCF and LCM
concepts.text: HCF uses common primes with least powers; LCM uses every prime with the greatest required power.

formulas: For two positive numbers: HCF × LCM = product
Divisible by 2, 5 or 10: last digit is even, 0 or 5, or 0 respectively
Divisible by 3 or 9: test the digit sum; divisible by 6: test both 2 and 3
Divisible by 4: test the last two digits
Divisible by 8: test the last three digits
Divisible by 11: alternating-place sums differ by a multiple of 11
method: Simplify brackets from the innermost pair outward.
Apply the relevant divisibility test before dividing.
Write each number as a product of primes.
Select least common powers for HCF and greatest required powers for LCM, then verify.

example.question: Find the HCF and LCM of 48 and 180.

practice.question: Three lights flash every 8, 12 and 30 seconds. When next together?

tips: One is neither prime nor composite.
Use HCF for greatest equal groups and LCM for the next common occurrence.
For two numbers only, use the product relation as a final check.

notes.subtitle: Negative Numbers, Number Lines & Changes

concepts.title: Integers
concepts.text: Integers are …,−3,−2,−1,0,1,2,3,… . Negative integers describe values below a reference point, while positive integers describe values above it.

concepts.title: Position and order
concepts.text: Integers increase as we move right on a number line. Among negative integers, the one closer to zero is greater.

concepts.title: Opposites
concepts.text: A number and its additive inverse lie at equal distances on opposite sides of zero and have sum zero.

concepts.title: Addition and subtraction
concepts.text: A positive change moves right and a negative change moves left. Subtracting an integer is the same as adding its opposite.

formulas: If a lies left of b, then a<b
method: Identify the starting integer and mark it on a number line.
Rewrite subtraction as addition of the opposite when helpful.
Move right for a positive addend and left for a negative addend.
Check the final sign against the direction and context.

example.question: Find −6+11−8.
steps: Start at −6 and move 11 places right to 5.

practice.question: A lift starts at floor 4, descends 9 floors and rises 2 floors.

tips: Zero is an integer but is neither positive nor negative.
Farther left means smaller, even when both numbers are negative.
Keep the sign with each number when adding several changes.

notes.subtitle: Representation, Types & Cardinality

concepts.title: Well-defined collections
concepts.text: A set is a well-defined collection of distinct objects, called elements. A description such as “beautiful pictures” is not precise enough to define a set.

concepts.title: Representation
concepts.text: A set may be described in words, listed in roster form, or written in set-builder form using a rule.

concepts.title: Finite, infinite and empty
concepts.text: A finite set ends, an infinite set continues without end, and the empty set has no elements.

concepts.title: Cardinality
concepts.text: The cardinality n(A) counts the distinct elements of A. Repeated entries are counted only once, and order does not change the count.

formulas: x∈A means x is an element of A
x∉A means x is not an element of A
n(A)=number of distinct elements of A
method: Check that the collection is described unambiguously.
Choose descriptive, roster or set-builder form as requested.
Remove repeated entries when writing roster form.
Count distinct elements and classify the set as finite, infinite or empty.

example.question: Write the set of distinct letters in SCHOOL and find its cardinality.
steps: List the letters S, C, H, O, O, L.
Write the repeated O only once.
example.answer: A={S,C,H,O,L}; n(A)=5, so A is finite.

practice.question: Write the vowels in the English alphabet in roster form.
Classify the set of natural numbers.
Write the whole numbers less than 5 in roster form.
Give one example of an empty set.
practice.answer: For example, the set of months having 32 days

practice.question: Write {3,6,9,12} in set-builder form and find its cardinality.
practice.answer: {x:x is a positive multiple of 3 and x≤12}; cardinality 4

tips: Braces contain elements; ∅ has no element, but {∅} has one element.
Do not count a repeated element more than once.
Use an ellipsis only when the continuation rule is clear.

notes.subtitle: Equivalent Forms, Comparison & Operations

concepts.title: Meaning and representation
concepts.text: A fraction a/b represents a÷b and b equal parts of a whole, of which a parts are selected. Fractions can be shown pictorially or on a number line.

concepts.title: Forms of fractions
concepts.text: A proper fraction is less than 1; an improper fraction is at least 1 and can be rewritten as a whole or mixed number.

concepts.title: Equivalent and comparable
concepts.text: Equivalent fractions name the same value. To compare unlike fractions, use a common denominator or cross-products.

concepts.title: Operations
concepts.text: Add or subtract using a common denominator, multiply numerators and denominators, and divide by multiplying by the reciprocal.

method: Convert mixed numbers to improper fractions when operating.
For addition or subtraction, find a common denominator.
For multiplication or division, cancel common factors before multiplying.
Reduce the result and convert an improper answer to mixed form when useful.
tips: Never add denominators when adding fractions.
The reciprocal is used for division, not for addition or subtraction.
Estimate whether the answer should be below or above 1 before calculating.
